slides.0.subtitle: Service exams test judgement, not just movements
slides.1.title: How to answer scenario questions
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Listen first
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Confirm party size, dishes, budget and preferences, asking questions if needed; the fuller the information, the better the recommendation
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Offer options with reasons
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Give two or three options at different prices, each with a one-line pairing reason (acid cuts fat, sweet with salt, tannin with protein)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Handling problems
slides.1.highlights.2.content: For faulty wine, an out-of-stock item or an unhappy guest: apologise and confirm first, offer an alternative, then inform the manager; stay calm and never argue
slides.1.content: Scoring points in scenarios: needs, options, reasons, follow-up.
slides.2.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
Scenario 1: four guests have ordered oysters, roast chicken and steak and want just one bottle at a mid-range budget. What do you recommend and why?
First confirm preferences (red, white, sparkling) and budget
A “bridge” wine that works with both seafood and red meat is needed
E.g. a high-acid, low-tannin red (such as Pinot Noir) or a traditional-method sparkling wine
Reason: high tannin can make oysters taste metallic, while high acidity handles fat
Offer two options at different prices

First check whether the guests prefer red, white or sparkling, and their rough budget. One bottle for both oysters and steak needs a “bridge” wine: a high-acid, low-tannin red (such as Pinot Noir from Burgundy or Oregon) or a traditional-method sparkling wine. Tannic reds can taste metallic with oysters, while high acidity cuts the fat of the chicken and steak. Finally offer two options at different prices.
Scenario 2: you open a Vintage Port for guests and the cork breaks in the neck, with heavy sediment in the wine. What do you do?
Stay calm and explain the situation to the guests
Carefully remove the remaining cork (with a suitable tool if needed)
Decant through a strainer or muslin in front of a light to remove sediment and cork fragments
Check the wine is sound, then pour the host a taste
If the wine is damaged, offer a replacement or alternative

Stay calm and explain to the guests. Carefully remove the broken cork from the neck, using a tool suited to old corks if needed. Then decant in front of a light through a strainer or muslin to remove sediment and cork fragments. Once the wine is confirmed sound, pour the host a taste; if it is damaged, proactively offer a replacement or alternative.
Scenario 3: a guest has ordered a very spicy Thai dish and wants wine with it. What do you recommend and why?
Chilli heat amplifies alcohol burn and bitterness
Choose low alcohol and low tannin
A touch of sweetness tempers the heat
Concrete example: off-dry Riesling or an aromatic white
Avoid high-alcohol, tannic, heavily oaked reds

Chilli heat amplifies alcohol burn and bitterness, so choose a low-alcohol, low-tannin wine, and a touch of sweetness tempers the heat further. Off-dry Riesling (such as German Kabinett or Spätlese) or an aromatic white works well; avoid high-alcohol, tannic, heavily oaked reds.
